transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, it’s good to meet you too, Doctor. I suppose... well, I’m here because things at work have just gotten incredibly frustrating lately, and it's starting to cause a real problem on the floor. I’m a first-line supervisor in retail, you see. Have been for a good while. I got my bachelor's degree years ago and I’ve always prided myself on communication, running a tight ship, making sure the sales workers know exactly what they need to be doing before the doors open. 

But recently, it’s like... well, I came in because when I try to explain the inventory numbers to the team, or when I'm trying to go over the weekend schedule—which is always a massive headache to organize anyway with everyone wanting Saturdays off—my words just start jumping. I’ll start off talking about the delivery trucks out back, making sure they get unloaded properly, but then suddenly I'm talking about Thursdays, and then before I know it I'm bringing up the church grill from the Sunday cookout, and then I'm going on about my boss’s tone of voice when he called me about the pallets last week. 

It makes sense while I'm saying it, but I look at my employees and they just stand there holding their clipboards. They look at me like they absolutely can’t follow what I’m saying. They get these wide, blank eyes, like I lost them three sentences ago. And I try to backtrack to get us back to the inventory counts, but there's just so much I need to communicate to them and it all just keeps tangling together when I speak.
Have you been feeling unusually energized or high lately?

Energized? High? No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. Honestly, if anything, it’s the exact opposite. I’m just... I'm exhausted, Doctor. You have to understand, running a retail floor at my age—I'm 59, you know—it takes a lot out of you even on a good day. You’re constantly on your feet, walking the aisles, checking the end-caps to make sure the corporate promotional displays are set up exactly to the planogram, dealing with vendors coming in the back door... 

And lately, with all this trouble I've been having, with my words getting all tangled up and the employees just staring at me like I'm speaking a foreign language, well, it's incredibly draining. It takes so much mental effort just to get through a simple ten-minute morning huddle now. I go home at the end of my shift and I just want to collapse in my recliner. There's no extra energy, no feeling revved up or on top of the world or anything like that. I wake up at 5:30 AM every single morning, I have my one cup of black coffee—same routine I've had since I got my degree, really—and I just try to push through the day. 

So, no, definitely not energized. It's just a heavy, heavy feeling trying to keep the store running when I can't even get through the weekly numbers without my brain pulling my sentences in ten different directions. It just wears a person out.
Have you been hearing voices when no one else is around?

Voices? Like... people talking when there's nobody there? No, Doctor, I haven't heard anything like that. The store is loud enough as it is, you know? Between the overhead music—which corporate insists on playing the exact same playlist every single day, I swear I hear those same twelve pop songs in my sleep—and the registers beeping, and the stockroom carts clattering over the tile floors, there's always noise. But it's all real noise, if you know what I mean. 

When I'm alone, like when I finally get home and sit down in my recliner... no, it's quiet. Well, I mean, the refrigerator hums, and sometimes I hear the neighbor's dog, but no voices. My problem isn't hearing things that aren't there, it's just... it's just getting the things that *are* in my head out of my mouth in an order that makes sense to my team. Like I was saying about the inventory counts, I know the numbers, I have the spreadsheets right there on my clipboard, but when I open my mouth to say "we're short on the seasonal end-cap displays," it just spirals into something else entirely. But nobody is whispering to me or talking to me when I'm by myself, no. Just my own thoughts, getting tangled up.
Have you had a stroke or head injury recently?

A stroke? Or a head injury? No, no, definitely nothing like that. I haven't hit my head, haven't been in any accidents. The last time I was in a hospital for anything physical was, oh, it must have been when I had my gallbladder taken out back in... well, that was a long time ago. But recently? No. 

I mean, I'm careful at work. We have strict safety protocols in the stockroom, you know, OSHA guidelines and all that. You can't just have people leaving pallets lying around or stacking boxes too high, especially the heavy liquid detergent boxes, those are a nightmare if they tip over. I always make sure the team is wearing their back braces if they're doing heavy lifting, and I certainly don't go climbing the tall ladders myself anymore, not at my age. We have the younger guys for that. 

And as for a stroke... well, I haven't had any of those warning signs they talk about on the television commercials, you know? My face isn't drooping, I can raise both my arms just fine, my vision hasn't gone blurry. I haven't collapsed or felt numb on one side. It's really just my speech, just the way my sentences get all scrambled up when I'm trying to direct the floor staff. It's not that my mouth isn't working, it's that the ideas just... they just run into each other. But physically, my head is perfectly fine. No bumps, no bruises, no strokes. Just a lot of frustration.
Have you started believing that people are trying to harm you or plot against you?

Plotting against me? Harm me? No, Doctor, no, I don't think anyone is out to get me. I mean, retail is competitive, sure, and sometimes the district manager comes down hard on us if the shrink numbers are too high or if the payroll percentage creeps up past the target... but that's just business, you know? That's just the nature of the beast when you're managing a big box store. They want results, they want the shelves faced perfectly, they want the seasonal aisles flipped overnight from Halloween straight into Christmas, and they want it done with a skeleton crew. It's stressful, absolutely, and sometimes I feel like corporate is completely disconnected from the reality of what happens on the floor.

But as far as people actually trying to harm me? Or some kind of conspiracy against me personally? No, I don't feel that at all. The team I have, well, they're good kids mostly. A lot of college students working part-time, some older folks who just want to get out of the house. They get frustrated with me lately, sure, because of... well, because of what I've been telling you about, how my words just sort of derail when I'm trying to give them instructions. I can see it in their eyes, they get confused, maybe a little impatient when I start talking about the end-caps and suddenly I'm bringing up the pallet jack maintenance schedule in the middle of a sentence about promotional signage. But they aren't malicious. They aren't plotting anything. 

Even the vendors, the guys who deliver the soda and the chips, they can be pushy about getting prime shelf space, but that's just sales. Nobody is sneaking around trying to hurt me. My life is pretty simple, really. It's just the store, my recliner, my coffee... and this awful, awful trouble I'm having with my thoughts getting all jumbled up before they make it out of my mouth. But no, no plots, no enemies. Just a lot of confusion on my end.
Have you needed much less sleep than usual lately without feeling tired?

Sleep? Needing less sleep? No, I wouldn't say that at all. Honestly, if anything, I feel like I could use more sleep, what with how exhausting the days have been lately. I mean, my sleep schedule is pretty set in stone, you know? I usually try to be in bed by 10:30, maybe 11:00 at the latest, right after the late local news. I like to catch the weather report because it really affects our foot traffic at the store—if they're calling for snow, even just a dusting, everybody rushes in for rock salt and milk, and I have to make sure the front end is staffed for the rush. 

So I watch the news, I turn off the TV, and I'm usually up by 5:30 AM. My alarm goes off, and I have my routine. I make my coffee—just a standard drip maker, none of those fancy pod machines, I like the smell of the grounds in the morning—and I sit in my recliner for about twenty minutes just to wake up before I get in the shower. I get my solid six and a half, maybe seven hours most nights. And I definitely feel it if I don't. 

Like last week, the overnight crew had an issue with the alarm system—the motion sensor by the receiving doors kept tripping, and the monitoring company called me at 2:00 in the morning. By the time I got it sorted out over the phone with the shift lead and finally got back to sleep, it was almost 3:30. When my alarm went off at 5:30, I was dragging. I felt it all day long. I had to drink three cups of coffee in the breakroom just to keep my eyes open while I was trying to review the shrink report, and even then, my head felt heavy. So no, I definitely don't have that thing where I don't need sleep. I need it, and I'm tired just like anybody else if I don't get enough of it. It's just... the exhaustion makes the talking worse, I think. When I'm tired, the words get even more tangled up. But my sleep itself, the amount I need, that hasn't changed at all.
Have you been having trouble understanding what other people say to you?

Understanding other people? Oh, no, no trouble with that at all. My hearing is fine, and my comprehension is perfectly fine. I know exactly what everyone is saying to me. When the district manager calls and tells me we need to push the loyalty program harder because our store's sign-up rate dropped by two percent last quarter, I understand him loud and clear. When the cashiers tell me their registers are out of receipt paper, or a customer comes up to me looking for the automotive section, I know exactly what they want. 

It's actually very frustrating, you see, because I take in the information perfectly. I process it. Someone asks me a question, say, about where we moved the clearance items, and in my head, the answer is right there. I know they're on the back wall near the seasonal department. I understand their question completely. But then, when I open my mouth to tell them, the words that come out... well, they just aren't the ones I meant to say. Or they are, but they're mixed in with thoughts about the inventory sheets or the squeaky wheel on the flatbed cart I was just pushing. 

So the problem isn't coming in, it's going out. I'm taking everything in just fine. I read the company memos, I listen to the morning huddle, I hear the complaints about the breakroom refrigerator smelling like old tuna—which, by the way, I've asked them to clean out every Friday, but nobody ever does—and I understand all of it. Every single word. It's just my own words that are betraying me. So, no, understanding people isn't an issue at all. I just wish they could understand me as well as I understand them.
Have you had any seizures recently?

Seizures? No, no. I've never had a seizure. Not recently, not ever in my fifty-nine years. I mean, physically, I'm actually in pretty decent shape, all things considered. You know, working retail, you're on your feet all day. Those concrete floors with just that thin layer of commercial tile over them—they absolutely destroy your knees and your lower back over the years. I've got a bit of stiffness, sure, and sometimes if I'm helping unload a truck because the receiving department is short-staffed again, I'll definitely feel it the next morning in my lumbar. I take an ibuprofen and I'm fine. But seizures? No. 

Like, falling down and convulsing? Never. We actually had an incident at the store, oh, it must have been three or four years ago now, right before the Thanksgiving rush. A customer had a seizure right in the middle of the baking aisle. Aisle four. She just completely collapsed, knocked over a whole display of condensed milk and pie crusts. It was terrifying, to be completely honest with you. I had to sprint over there, we called 911 immediately, and I had my shift lead block off both ends of the aisle with shopping carts so people wouldn't crowd around her, and we just tried to make sure she didn't hit her head on the metal base decks of the shelving until the paramedics arrived. 

So I know what a seizure looks like, and I know how serious they can be. But no, I haven't had anything even remotely like that happen to me. My body works just fine, my heart is good, my blood pressure is usually fine... it's really just, well, like I was saying before, it's just the words that get all scrambled up on the way out. My brain doesn't shut down or make me shake or pass out or anything physical like that. Just the talking. So, no, definitely no seizures.
Do you often have trouble finding the exact word you want to say?

Finding the exact word? No, it's not really like that. It's not that I'm standing there snapping my fingers trying to remember if it's called a 'pallet jack' or a 'hand truck.' I know the words. My vocabulary is perfectly fine, I've got a bachelor's degree in business administration, I know how to speak. 

It's more like... well, like I was saying before, it's not that I can't find the word, it's that the wrong ones come out with it, or they all come out at once. Like yesterday, I was trying to tell my assistant manager, Dave—Dave's a good kid, been with us two years, but he needs a lot of direction—I was trying to tell him to make sure the endcaps were faced before closing. And in my head, the sentence was, 'Dave, please face the endcaps.' Simple, right? But what came out was something like, 'Dave, face the endcaps, the truck is late, the squeaky wheel on the cart, the tuna in the fridge.' It just... spilled out. All these thoughts that were in my head, they just latched onto the sentence I was trying to say. 

So the words I want are there, I don't have trouble finding them. They just get buried under everything else. It's incredibly frustrating because I can see the look on people's faces when it happens. Dave just stared at me for a second, then nodded and walked away, and I knew he didn't understand the part that actually mattered. But no, I don't sit there forgetting the names of things or struggling to find a specific word. The words are all there. There's just too many of them trying to get out the door at the same time, if that makes sense. Like a bottleneck at the registers on a Saturday afternoon when you only have two cashiers scheduled. You know what needs to happen, you know who needs to go where, but it's just a mess.
Did these speech problems start suddenly?

Suddenly? No, no, it wasn't like a light switch flipping off, or on, I suppose. It wasn't like I woke up one Tuesday and suddenly couldn't give Dave a straight instruction about the endcaps. It's been more of a... a gradual slide, I guess you could say. Like a slow leak in a tire. You don't notice it right away, but eventually, you're driving on the rim. 

I'd say it's been going on for about six months now. That's when I really started noticing it, or at least, that's when it became impossible to ignore. Because before that, maybe I'd have a little slip of the tongue, or I'd lose my train of thought for a second—which happens to everyone, right? Especially when you're managing a floor with twenty different things happening at once. But about six months ago, that's when the jumbled explanations really started. I'd be trying to explain the new return policy to a customer—corporate changed it from thirty days to forty-five, but only with a receipt, and only for certain departments, which is a nightmare to enforce, let me tell you—and I'd just start throwing in things about the floor buffer being broken or the delivery truck being delayed at the distribution center. 

And then there are the stops. The odd stops. I'll just be walking across the sales floor, heading from the backroom to the customer service desk to approve a void, and I'll just... stop. Right in the middle of the main action alley. And it's not because I saw a spill that needed cleaning or a display that was knocked over. I just stop because the words and the thoughts are all crashing together in my head, and I have to physically halt just to try and sort them out. It's been about half a year of this. Six months of people looking at me like I've grown a second head while I stand there in front of the seasonal aisle trying to untangle my own sentences. So, no, definitely not sudden. Just a slow, incredibly frustrating build-up over the last six months.
Have you been feeling emotionally flat or less able to show feelings than usual?

Emotionally flat? Less able to show feelings? No, I wouldn't say that at all. If anything, I feel things too much right now, mostly just sheer frustration. I mean, how could you not be frustrated when you can't even get a simple sentence out without it turning into a complete disaster? 

I definitely still have feelings. I get angry, I get annoyed—especially with corporate and their ridiculous policy changes that they expect us to enforce on the floor without giving us the payroll to actually staff the registers. I get happy, too. Like when my granddaughter comes over on Sundays, I feel that. I smile, I laugh with her. She's three, she's at that age where everything is funny to her, and it's impossible not to feel joy around that. 

But at work? The dominant feeling is just... stress. And embarrassment. When I'm standing there in front of Dave or a customer, and the words start piling up like a multi-car pileup on the interstate, I feel my face get hot. I feel my heart rate go up. I feel the humiliation of knowing they're looking at me, a fifty-nine-year-old man who's been managing this store for over a decade, wondering if I'm losing my mind. 

So, no, I'm not flat. I'm not walking around like a zombie or a robot. I still feel everything just as sharply as I always have. It's just that right now, most of what I'm feeling is incredibly negative because of this... this communication issue. If I could just talk normally, if I could just say, 'Dave, face the endcaps,' without throwing in the tuna and the squeaky cart, I'd probably feel a lot better. But the feelings themselves? They're all still there, loud and clear. Maybe even a little too loud sometimes.
Have you been more active than usual lately, taking on lots of projects or doing much more than you normally would?

More active? Taking on extra projects? Oh, absolutely not. No, I don't know where I'd even find the time or the energy for something like that, let alone the focus, given everything else going on with my speech. By the time I get home from the store, my feet are just aching—standing on that polished concrete for nine or ten hours a day, it really does a number on your knees and your lower back when you're fifty-nine. I usually just collapse into my armchair in the living room and turn on the television, though half the time I don't even really watch it, it's just background noise while I try to decompress from the day.

So no, no new projects. I haven't suddenly decided to remodel the kitchen or build a deck or take up woodworking or anything crazy like that. Just keeping up with the bare minimum at work feels like a mountain right now. I mean, corporate just sent down the new planograms for the back-to-school reset—which is ridiculous because it's barely summer, but retail is always two seasons ahead—and usually I'd be all over that. I'd be getting the gondolas moved and mapping out the shelf strips before the freight even arrives. But lately? I just handed the binder to Dave and told him to do his best. Which, honestly, is probably going to end up a disaster knowing him, but I just don't have the drive to micromanage it right now. 

Between trying to untangle my own sentences all day and just keeping the doors open with our current payroll budget, I'm completely exhausted. I'm doing exactly what I have to do to keep the store running, and not an ounce more. If anything, I'm probably doing a little less than I used to, just because it takes so much mental energy to get through a simple conversation with a vendor or a customer without making a fool of myself. So, no, definitely not bouncing off the walls or taking on anything extra. Just trying to survive the daily grind, really.
Have you had any new medical problems in the last six months?

New medical problems? No, no, nothing like that. My health has been pretty much the same as it's been for the last, oh, I don't know, maybe five or six years. I mean, I have the usual things you'd expect for a guy my age who spends all day on his feet. Like I mentioned, my lower back acts up, especially if I have to help unload a truck because someone called out sick—which happens entirely too often these days. And my knees, well, they aren't what they used to be when I was playing softball in my thirties, but I take a little ibuprofen in the morning with my coffee and that usually takes the edge off enough to get me through a shift. 

But as for anything new? Anything in the last six months? No, sir. I haven't been sick, haven't had a fever, haven't been to the hospital or even my regular doctor, except for my annual physical back in... I think it was October. Or maybe early November. Before the big Thanksgiving rush, anyway. And my doctor said everything looked fine then. Blood pressure was a little elevated, but he said that was probably just the stress of retail during the holidays, which is completely understandable. My cholesterol was okay, blood sugar was fine. 

I haven't had any injuries either, thank goodness. You know, we have these safety meetings at work every month—corporate makes us watch these incredibly cheesy videos about ladder safety and proper lifting techniques, and I always roll my eyes, but I do follow the rules. I haven't slipped, haven't fallen, haven't hit my head or anything like that. I know sometimes people ask about hitting your head when you start having trouble talking, but I haven't. I'm very careful, especially in the stockroom where things can get a bit precarious if the night crew hasn't stacked the pallets right. 

So, physically, medically, I'm just exactly the same as I was before all this speech nonsense started. Just a fifty-nine-year-old guy with achy joints and a stressful job. Nothing new at all on the medical front. Just... just the words getting all tangled up. That's the only new thing, and believe me, that's more than enough for me to deal with right now.
When you speak, do other people tell you that your thoughts jump from one topic to another in a way that is hard to follow?

Well, they don't always have to actually *say* it out loud, Doctor, because I can see it right there on their faces. But yes, that is... honestly, that's the main reason I came in to see you in the first place. It’s exactly that. 

I’ll be standing there in the back room, right by the time clock or the bulletin board, and I’ll be trying to do something incredibly simple. Just trying to explain the inventory numbers for the week, or maybe going over the weekend schedule with the team. Because the weekend schedule is always a nightmare, you know? You have part-timers who suddenly need Saturday off, or we're short on payroll, so it takes a lot of careful coordination to make sure the floor is covered. 

So I'll start out fine. I'll start talking about the delivery trucks, because we need to know when the trucks are arriving so we can schedule the unloaders. But then, before I can even finish the point I was trying to make, my words just... they start jumping all over the place. I’ll go from the trucks to talking about Thursdays, because Thursday is our big delivery day, but then instead of staying on the schedule, I’m suddenly talking about the church grill. Just out of absolutely nowhere! The grill from the church cookout. And then from the church grill, my mouth is suddenly going off about my district manager—my boss—and the tone he used with me on our last conference call. Which, by the way, was incredibly condescending, he always has this tone like we're all incompetent just because we're working the store level while he's sitting in some cushy corporate office. 

But the point is, none of that has anything to do with the weekend schedule or the inventory! And I know it doesn't, or at least I realize it as it's happening, but the words just keep tumbling out, jumping from one completely unrelated thing to another. Trucks, Thursdays, the church grill, my boss's tone. Just skipping tracks. And I look at Dave, or whoever I'm trying to give directions to, and they are just staring at me. They look at me like they absolutely cannot follow what I’m saying. 

It’s humiliating, frankly. You can see the exact moment they lose the thread. Their eyes kind of glaze over, or they get this tight, uncomfortable little smile, and they're just waiting for me to stop talking because my thoughts are bouncing around like a pinball machine. It makes me look like I don't know how to run my own store, which couldn't be further from the truth, I've been doing this for years. But when the words come out like that... yeah. People definitely notice it.
Have you started believing things that other people say are not true, even though they feel completely real to you?

Believing things that aren't true? No, no, definitely not. I've always been a very practical, grounded sort of person, Doctor. You really have to be when you're running a retail store. You deal in facts and figures, not imagination. I mean, if the weekly sales report says we're down four percent compared to this same week last year, that's just a hard fact. I can't just pretend we had a great week because I feel like it, you know? The numbers are the numbers, the inventory is the inventory. If the computer system says we have twelve cordless drills in stock and the shelf is completely empty, well, that's a reality I have to deal with, which usually means someone walked right out the front doors with them while we were short-staffed. 

So, no, I haven't been having any strange ideas or believing things that aren't real. Frankly, it's usually the other way around, where I'm the one having to tell my employees what's real and what isn't. Like just last week, one of the new cashiers, a young kid, maybe nineteen years old, tried to tell me over the phone that he couldn't come in for his closing shift because his car broke down on the interstate. But the thing is, I had literally just seen him pulling into the drive-thru at the burger place across the street when I was walking back from my own lunch
During these times when your speech gets jumbled, have you also been feeling unusually cheerful, euphoric, or on top of the world?

Cheerful? Euphoric? Oh, gosh, no. No, not even a little bit. I mean, honestly, Doctor, how could anybody possibly feel cheerful when they can't even get a simple sentence out straight? If anything, it's the exact opposite of that. It is incredibly frustrating. 

I'm standing there, trying to run a busy retail store, which, let me tell you, is stressful enough on a good day. You've got customers complaining about inflation, corporate breathing down your neck about loyalty card sign-ups—which is a whole other headache because absolutely nobody wants to sign up for another store credit card right now with interest rates being what they are—and then, on top of all that daily pressure, I can't even communicate basic instructions to my own team. 

So, no, I definitely do not feel "on top of the world." I feel like I'm sinking, if I'm being completely honest with you. I've always taken a lot of pride in being in control, you know? In being the guy who has the answers when things go wrong on the floor. When the registers go down or a truck is delayed, my employees look to me to fix it. And now, I open my mouth to fix it and I just sound like a complete fool. It makes me feel anxious, and maybe a bit angry at myself, and mostly just exhausted. But definitely not happy or euphoric. 

When those moments happen, I just want the floor to swallow me up. I just want to get through my shift without humiliating myself, clock out, go home, sit in my recliner, and just... not have to talk to anyone for a few hours. There is absolutely nothing cheerful about what's happening to my speech, I can promise you that. It's just a miserable, embarrassing experience every single time it happens.
Have you been having problems with your memory?

Memory problems? No, no, I wouldn't say that. My memory is actually pretty sharp, all things considered. I mean, you kind of have to have a steel trap for a memory in my line of work, Doctor. When you're managing a retail store, especially one the size of ours, there are a million little details you have to keep track of every single day. 

Just yesterday, for example, I remembered that we had a specific model of a space heater—the ceramic tower ones with the remote control, not the oscillating base ones—tucked away in the top steel of the backroom from last winter. A customer came in looking for one, and the floor associate, bless his heart, told her we were entirely sold out because the home heating aisle was bare. But I remembered. I remembered exactly where it was, third pallet rack down, right side, behind a display of seasonal wrapping paper we hadn't pulled down yet. I got the ladder, climbed up there, and pulled it down for her myself. She was thrilled, absolutely thrilled. 

And it's not just inventory. I remember employee schedules, I remember vendor delivery windows. I can tell you that the Pepsi guy always comes on Tuesdays between ten and noon, but he's usually running late if it rained the day before because his route takes him through that low-water crossing out on County Road 9. I remember all of that. 

So, no, the memory itself is fine. It’s just... it’s just the speaking part. The getting the thoughts out of my head and into the air part. It's like the filing cabinets in my brain are perfectly organized, every file is right where it should be, but when I open the drawer to pull one out, a gust of wind just blows all the papers around the room. I know what I want to say, I remember exactly what I need to communicate, but the words just get entirely jumbled up on the way out of my mouth. But the memory itself? No, no issues there at all. I can still remember the PLU code for organic bananas from when I worked produce fifteen years ago—it's 94011, by the way. Regular is 4011, organic always has the 9 in front. You never forget things like that.
Apart from the trouble with speaking, have you been having a harder time managing your usual work or daily responsibilities?

Well... yes. Yes, I suppose I have been, if I'm being completely honest about it all. It's... it's been getting really difficult, Doctor, and it's starting to have some pretty serious consequences at the store. 

You see, I've been a supervisor for a long time. I know the rhythms of retail, I know how to handle the rush. Usually, I'm the guy they want on the floor during the busiest times—Saturday afternoons, holiday weekends, the back-to-school rush in August. I thrive on that chaos, usually. But lately... well, lately, my district manager, Mr. Henderson, he's been pulling me off the schedule for those busy weekend shifts. He says it's because I'm "struggling to communicate effectively under pressure," which, I mean, I guess is true with the way my words get all tangled up, but it really hurts, you know? Being sidelined like that. I'm not trusted to run those busy weekend shifts anymore. They've got the assistant manager, Sarah—she's only been with us for two years—handling the Saturday morning open now. 

And it's not just the schedule changes. We had my quarterly performance review about three weeks ago, and it was... it was rough. Mr. Henderson sat me down in the back office, closed the door—which is never a good sign—and he actually warned me. He said that if things don't improve, if I can't start communicating clearly with the team and the customers again, I could be suspended. Suspended! After all the years I've put into that company, the late nights, the inventory counts, the covering for people who just don't show up... to be told I might be suspended because my brain won't let my mouth work right. It's terrifying, honestly. I've got a mortgage, I've got car payments. I can't afford to be suspended.

And it's spilling over into my home life, too, which is just as frustrating. My wife, Linda, she's had to start picking up a lot of the slack for things I used to handle without a second thought. Like, I used to be the one who went to the neighborhood watch meetings on the first Thursday of the month, or I'd be the one to call the contractor when the gutters needed cleaning. But lately, when I try to do those things, when I try to talk to people... they just get this look on their face. This sort of polite, confused, slightly uncomfortable look. Like they're trying to figure out if I'm drunk or having a stroke or something. It's humiliating. So Linda has had to start covering those commitments for me, just to avoid the awkwardness. She's been wonderful about it, really she has, but I can tell it's wearing on her, having to be my... my translator, I guess you could say, to the rest of the world. So, yes, it's definitely making it a lot harder to manage my responsibilities, both at work and at home.
Have you been seeing things that other people do not see?

Seeing things? Like... hallucinations? No, no, absolutely not. My eyes are perfectly fine, Doctor. Like I mentioned, my lower back acts up, especially if I have to help unload a truck because someone called out sick—which happens entirely too often these days. And my knees, well, they aren't what they used to be when I was playing softball in my thirties, but I take a little ibuprofen in the morning with my coffee and that usually takes the edge off enough to get me through a shift. 

But as for anything new? Anything in the last six months? No, sir. I haven't been sick, haven't had a fever, haven't been to the hospital or even my regular doctor, except for my annual physical back in... I think it was October. Or maybe early November. Before the big Thanksgiving rush, anyway. And my doctor said everything looked fine then. Blood pressure was a little elevated, but he said that was probably just the stress of retail during the holidays, which is completely understandable. My cholesterol was okay, blood sugar was fine. 

I haven't had any injuries either, thank goodness. You know, we have these safety meetings at work every month—corporate makes us watch these incredibly cheesy videos about ladder safety and proper lifting techniques, and I always roll my eyes, but I do follow the rules. I haven't slipped, haven't fallen, haven't hit my head or anything like that. I know sometimes people ask about hitting your head when you start having trouble talking, but I haven't. I'm very careful, especially in the stockroom where things can get a bit precarious if the night crew hasn't stacked the pallets right. 

So, physically, medically, I'm just exactly the same as I was before all this speech nonsense started. Just a fifty-nine-year-old guy with achy joints and a stressful job. Nothing new at all on the medical front. Just... just the words getting all tangled up. That's the only new thing, and believe me, that's more than enough for me to deal with right now.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is a formal thought disorder with tangentiality/derailment independent of mood or psychosis, which would most strongly support schizophrenia over schizoaffective disorder, bipolar mania, or a medical/organic psychotic disorder.
doctor.question: When you speak, do other people tell you that your thoughts jump from one topic to another in a way that is hard to follow?

target_item.name: Disorganized_Thinking_Speech
target_item.manifestation: I came in because when I try to explain inventory numbers or the weekend schedule, my words start jumping from trucks to Thursdays to the church grill to my boss’s tone, and people look at me like they can’t follow what I’m saying.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question directly asks about thoughts jumping from one topic to another making it hard to follow, which matches the definition and manifestation of disorganized thinking and speech.

patient.answer:
Well, they don't always have to actually *say* it out loud, Doctor, because I can see it right there on their faces. But yes, that is... honestly, that's the main reason I came in to see you in the first place. It’s exactly that. 

I’ll be standing there in the back room, right by the time clock or the bulletin board, and I’ll be trying to do something incredibly simple. Just trying to explain the inventory numbers for the week, or maybe going over the weekend schedule with the team. Because the weekend schedule is always a nightmare, you know? You have part-timers who suddenly need Saturday off, or we're short on payroll, so it takes a lot of careful coordination to make sure the floor is covered. 

So I'll start out fine. I'll start talking about the delivery trucks, because we need to know when the trucks are arriving so we can schedule the unloaders. But then, before I can even finish the point I was trying to make, my words just... they start jumping all over the place. I’ll go from the trucks to talking about Thursdays, because Thursday is our big delivery day, but then instead of staying on the schedule, I’m suddenly talking about the church grill. Just out of absolutely nowhere! The grill from the church cookout. And then from the church grill, my mouth is suddenly going off about my district manager—my boss—and the tone he used with me on our last conference call. Which, by the way, was incredibly condescending, he always has this tone like we're all incompetent just because we're working the store level while he's sitting in some cushy corporate office. 

But the point is, none of that has anything to do with the weekend schedule or the inventory! And I know it doesn't, or at least I realize it as it's happening, but the words just keep tumbling out, jumping from one completely unrelated thing to another. Trucks, Thursdays, the church grill, my boss's tone. Just skipping tracks. And I look at Dave, or whoever I'm trying to give directions to, and they are just staring at me. They look at me like they absolutely cannot follow what I’m saying. 

It’s humiliating, frankly. You can see the exact moment they lose the thread. Their eyes kind of glaze over, or they get this tight, uncomfortable little smile, and they're just waiting for me to stop talking because my thoughts are bouncing around like a pinball machine. It makes me look like I don't know how to run my own store, which couldn't be further from the truth, I've been doing this for years. But when the words come out like that... yeah. People definitely notice it.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there are clear delusions or bizarre false beliefs, which would support schizophrenia-spectrum illness over mania and help distinguish from a neurologic/organic language disorder.
doctor.question: Have you started believing things that other people say are not true, even though they feel completely real to you?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about delusions, which are false beliefs, but my symptom profile only includes disorganized thinking/speech, disorganized abnormal behavior, functional impairment, and duration. It does not include delusions.

patient.answer:
Believing things that aren't true? No, no, definitely not. I've always been a very practical, grounded sort of person, Doctor. You really have to be when you're running a retail store. You deal in facts and figures, not imagination. I mean, if the weekly sales report says we're down four percent compared to this same week last year, that's just a hard fact. I can't just pretend we had a great week because I feel like it, you know? The numbers are the numbers, the inventory is the inventory. If the computer system says we have twelve cordless drills in stock and the shelf is completely empty, well, that's a reality I have to deal with, which usually means someone walked right out the front doors with them while we were short-staffed. 

So, no, I haven't been having any strange ideas or believing things that aren't real. Frankly, it's usually the other way around, where I'm the one having to tell my employees what's real and what isn't. Like just last week, one of the new cashiers, a young kid, maybe nineteen years old, tried to tell me over the phone that he couldn't come in for his closing shift because his car broke down on the interstate. But the thing is, I had literally just seen him pulling into the drive-thru at the burger place across the street when I was walking back from my own lunch

doctor.intent: Determine whether the disorganized speech occurs only during mood elevation or in the absence of mood symptoms, to distinguish schizophrenia from schizoaffective disorder and mania.
doctor.question: During these times when your speech gets jumbled, have you also been feeling unusually cheerful, euphoric, or on top of the world?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of mania, such as feeling unusually cheerful, euphoric, or on top of the world. My symptom profile does not include any information about manic symptoms.

patient.answer:
Cheerful? Euphoric? Oh, gosh, no. No, not even a little bit. I mean, honestly, Doctor, how could anybody possibly feel cheerful when they can't even get a simple sentence out straight? If anything, it's the exact opposite of that. It is incredibly frustrating. 

I'm standing there, trying to run a busy retail store, which, let me tell you, is stressful enough on a good day. You've got customers complaining about inflation, corporate breathing down your neck about loyalty card sign-ups—which is a whole other headache because absolutely nobody wants to sign up for another store credit card right now with interest rates being what they are—and then, on top of all that daily pressure, I can't even communicate basic instructions to my own team. 

So, no, I definitely do not feel "on top of the world." I feel like I'm sinking, if I'm being completely honest with you. I've always taken a lot of pride in being in control, you know? In being the guy who has the answers when things go wrong on the floor. When the registers go down or a truck is delayed, my employees look to me to fix it. And now, I open my mouth to fix it and I just sound like a complete fool. It makes me feel anxious, and maybe a bit angry at myself, and mostly just exhausted. But definitely not happy or euphoric. 

When those moments happen, I just want the floor to swallow me up. I just want to get through my shift without humiliating myself, clock out, go home, sit in my recliner, and just... not have to talk to anyone for a few hours. There is absolutely nothing cheerful about what's happening to my speech, I can promise you that. It's just a miserable, embarrassing experience every single time it happens.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is objective cognitive decline beyond disorganized speech, which would favor an organic etiology over primary psychotic or mood disorders.
doctor.question: Have you been having problems with your memory?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about memory problems, which is not covered by any of the items in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Memory problems? No, no, I wouldn't say that. My memory is actually pretty sharp, all things considered. I mean, you kind of have to have a steel trap for a memory in my line of work, Doctor. When you're managing a retail store, especially one the size of ours, there are a million little details you have to keep track of every single day. 

Just yesterday, for example, I remembered that we had a specific model of a space heater—the ceramic tower ones with the remote control, not the oscillating base ones—tucked away in the top steel of the backroom from last winter. A customer came in looking for one, and the floor associate, bless his heart, told her we were entirely sold out because the home heating aisle was bare. But I remembered. I remembered exactly where it was, third pallet rack down, right side, behind a display of seasonal wrapping paper we hadn't pulled down yet. I got the ladder, climbed up there, and pulled it down for her myself. She was thrilled, absolutely thrilled. 

And it's not just inventory. I remember employee schedules, I remember vendor delivery windows. I can tell you that the Pepsi guy always comes on Tuesdays between ten and noon, but he's usually running late if it rained the day before because his route takes him through that low-water crossing out on County Road 9. I remember all of that. 

So, no, the memory itself is fine. It’s just... it’s just the speaking part. The getting the thoughts out of my head and into the air part. It's like the filing cabinets in my brain are perfectly organized, every file is right where it should be, but when I open the drawer to pull one out, a gust of wind just blows all the papers around the room. I know what I want to say, I remember exactly what I need to communicate, but the words just get entirely jumbled up on the way out of my mouth. But the memory itself? No, no issues there at all. I can still remember the PLU code for organic bananas from when I worked produce fifteen years ago—it's 94011, by the way. Regular is 4011, organic always has the 9 in front. You never forget things like that.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is any decline in everyday functioning beyond speech, which would help distinguish schizophrenia from schizoaffective disorder, bipolar disorder, and a primary medical/organic psychosis.
doctor.question: Apart from the trouble with speaking, have you been having a harder time managing your usual work or daily responsibilities?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’m not trusted to run busy weekend shifts anymore, and after the performance review my boss warned me I could be suspended if things don’t improve. At home, my wife has had to cover commitments I used to handle because people started getting uncomfortable or confused around me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the impact of the symptoms on the patient's work and daily responsibilities, which directly corresponds to the functional impairment item in the symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well... yes. Yes, I suppose I have been, if I'm being completely honest about it all. It's... it's been getting really difficult, Doctor, and it's starting to have some pretty serious consequences at the store. 

You see, I've been a supervisor for a long time. I know the rhythms of retail, I know how to handle the rush. Usually, I'm the guy they want on the floor during the busiest times—Saturday afternoons, holiday weekends, the back-to-school rush in August. I thrive on that chaos, usually. But lately... well, lately, my district manager, Mr. Henderson, he's been pulling me off the schedule for those busy weekend shifts. He says it's because I'm "struggling to communicate effectively under pressure," which, I mean, I guess is true with the way my words get all tangled up, but it really hurts, you know? Being sidelined like that. I'm not trusted to run those busy weekend shifts anymore. They've got the assistant manager, Sarah—she's only been with us for two years—handling the Saturday morning open now. 

And it's not just the schedule changes. We had my quarterly performance review about three weeks ago, and it was... it was rough. Mr. Henderson sat me down in the back office, closed the door—which is never a good sign—and he actually warned me. He said that if things don't improve, if I can't start communicating clearly with the team and the customers again, I could be suspended. Suspended! After all the years I've put into that company, the late nights, the inventory counts, the covering for people who just don't show up... to be told I might be suspended because my brain won't let my mouth work right. It's terrifying, honestly. I've got a mortgage, I've got car payments. I can't afford to be suspended.

And it's spilling over into my home life, too, which is just as frustrating. My wife, Linda, she's had to start picking up a lot of the slack for things I used to handle without a second thought. Like, I used to be the one who went to the neighborhood watch meetings on the first Thursday of the month, or I'd be the one to call the contractor when the gutters needed cleaning. But lately, when I try to do those things, when I try to talk to people... they just get this look on their face. This sort of polite, confused, slightly uncomfortable look. Like they're trying to figure out if I'm drunk or having a stroke or something. It's humiliating. So Linda has had to start covering those commitments for me, just to avoid the awkwardness. She's been wonderful about it, really she has, but I can tell it's wearing on her, having to be my... my translator, I guess you could say, to the rest of the world. So, yes, it's definitely making it a lot harder to manage my responsibilities, both at work and at home.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there are visual hallucinations to distinguish a primary psychotic disorder from a possible organic psychosis, since auditory hallucinations and delusions have been denied and mania appears unlikely.
doctor.question: Have you been seeing things that other people do not see?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about visual hallucinations (seeing things others do not see), which is not part of my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Seeing things? Like... hallucinations? No, no, absolutely not. My eyes are perfectly fine, Doctor. Well, I mean, I wear bifocals now, which I had to get about three years ago because reading the tiny print on the inventory SKUs was giving me terrible headaches. You know those little yellow tags they use for the seasonal clearance items? The font on those has to be a size six, at best, and under those awful fluorescent lights we have in the store, it's just an absolute nightmare for your retinas. But as far as seeing things that aren't actually there? No, never. 

If anything, I see more of what's actually there than anyone else on my team. In retail, you have to have eyes in the back of your head, you really do. Just the other day, I spotted a teenager trying to slip a pair of those expensive Bluetooth earbuds into his hoodie pocket from three aisles over. The loss prevention guy, Dave—who is half my age, by the way, and supposedly trained for exactly this kind of thing—was looking right at the security monitors and completely missed it. He was probably checking his phone, if we're being honest. But I saw it plain as day. 

I see the store, I see the customers, I see the dust on the top shelves that the night crew keeps ignoring—which I’ve left three separate notes about, by the way, but that's a whole different battle. I see it all exactly as it is. There are no visions, no mirages, no imaginary people walking around my store. It all comes back to just this incredibly frustrating inability to get the words out of my mouth when I need to tell someone about what I'm looking at. So, no, definitely no issues with my vision or seeing things that aren't there.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is objective evidence of a primary neurologic disorder causing the disorganized speech, which would favor an organic psychotic disorder over schizophrenia-spectrum or bipolar conditions.
doctor.question: Have you had any brain imaging, like an MRI or CT scan, for this problem?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about medical tests (brain imaging like MRI or CT scan), which is not covered by any of the provided symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
Brain imaging? Like... an MRI, in one of those big magnetic tubes? No, no, I haven't had anything like that done. Nobody has ordered one or even brought it up until now. 

You see, I started with my regular primary care physician, Dr. Evans—I’ve been going to him for, oh, it has to be fifteen years now. His office is right over in that medical plaza next to where the old Sears used to be before they tore it down to build those new luxury apartments. Anyway, Linda—my wife—she finally insisted I go see him because of the whole... the words getting stuck and jumbled issue, especially after Mr. Henderson gave me that warning at work. So I took an extended lunch break on a Thursday, which I absolutely hate doing because Thursdays are when we get our main pallet deliveries for the weekend, and if I'm not there to supervise the offloading, the stock boys just dump everything in the main aisles and leave it there for the customers to trip over. 

But I went to see Dr. Evans, and I tried my best to explain what was happening, how the thoughts are perfectly clear in my head but the words just come out entirely wrong. And he did the standard physical, you know, checked my blood pressure, listened to my heart, looked in my ears with the little light, but he didn't mention anything about a CT scan or an MRI or taking pictures of my brain. He just said I needed to see someone who specializes in... well, in this sort of thing, and he gave me the referral to your clinic. 

Which is fine by me, honestly, because I don't even know how I'd find the time to go sit in a hospital or an imaging center for a scan right now. We're gearing up for the end-of-quarter inventory counts, and I can't be away from the store for half the day to lay inside a machine that sounds like a washing machine full of wrenches. That's what my brother-in-law Gary said it sounded like, anyway, when he had his knee done last year after he slipped on his icy driveway. He said it was incredibly loud and claustrophobic. So, no. No scans, no brain imaging. Just the regular physical with Dr. Evans and then coming straight here to talk to you.
